corrected_value.title: A sequence variant in ZFHX3 on 16q22 associates with atrial fibrillation and ischemic stroke

decisions.quote: We also replicated 16q22 (ZFHX3) as a risk locus for CE (OR = 1.62 for the T allele; 95% CI, 1.26–2.07, p = 0.0014) and found this locus significantly associated with overall IS (OR = 1.28 for the T allele; 95% CI, 1.12–1.47, p = 0.002) (Table 1).
decisions.location: Results (Association of candidate stroke risk variants with stroke and stroke subtypes), Table 1, and Reference 10
decisions.reason: The paper explicitly selects and empirically re-tests the 16q22 (ZFHX3, rs7193343) stroke susceptibility locus originally reported by Gudbjartsson et al. (2009, Nat. Genet. 41:876-878, DOI 10.1038/ng.417; Reference 10 in Table 1) in a Spanish cohort of 2,968 cases and 3,772 controls. This original study is completely distinct from shipped rows 2412 (Bellenguez et al., 2012, 10.1038/ng.1081, HDAC9) and 2504 (Holliday et al., 2012, 10.1038/ng.2397, 6p21.1) and from all other candidate target indices in this paper.

decisions.quote:
The Lagged Score “Placebo” Test


       There is no control for the change in student baseline scores in Equation (5). Like CFR,

we are effectively assuming that the change in predicted value-added is exogenous to any change

in baseline achievement. In a recent paper, Rothstein (2014) reports a statistically significant

relationship between change in teacher value-added and changes in baseline achievement as

prima facie evidence of bias in the CFR method. We find similar results, but offer a different

interpretation. We find that the predicted change has a coefficient of .268 when lagged scores

are the dependent variable.
decisions.location: Introduction (p. 3), Section "The Lagged Score ‘Placebo’ Test" (pp. 19-21), Table 5, and References (p. 34)
decisions.reason: The paper explicitly states in the Introduction ("In addition to replicating the CFR and Rothstein analyses, we extended their work in three ways") and in the section "The Lagged Score ‘Placebo’ Test" (pp. 19-21, Table 5) that it replicates and re-tests Jesse Rothstein's (2014, "Revisiting the Impacts of Teachers") lagged baseline-score placebo test on LAUSD teacher switches. This work is distinct from shipped row 609 (Chetty, Friedman, and Rockoff, 2014, 10.1257/aer.104.9.2593) and has no DOI in the source text.

corrected_value.authors: Roter, D. L., Hall, J. A., Katz, N. R.
corrected_value.title: Relations between physicians’ behaviors and analogue patients’ satisfaction, recall and impressions

decisions.quote:
In the last of her two papers about the
relative relevance of instrumental or task-re-
lated behavior on one hand, and socio-emo-
tional or affective behavior on the other,
Roter called on other researchers “‘to repli-
cate her findings through different method-
ologies and in the natural setting.’”* This call
was based on two possible weaknesses of
her study: 1) the use of simulated patients
instead of real patients, which raises ques-
tions about the generalization of the results,
and 2) the use of audiotapes instead of video-
tapes, which limited the possibility to regis-
ter nonverbal affect to vocal-tone, only. Our
study can be seen as such a replication: it
took place in the natural setting (real general
practitioners with real patients who had hy-
pertension) and used partly different meth-
odologies (video instead of audio, which
made it possible to register visual as well vo-
cal cues).
decisions.reason: The Discussion explicitly frames the study as a replication answering the call in the second of the two 1987 companion papers (Reference 8: Roter DL, Hall JA, Katz NR, "Relations between physicians’ behaviors and analogue patients’ satisfaction, recall and impressions", Med Care 1987;25:437) and compares findings across the previous RIAS studies. Shipped row 649 represents only the first companion article (Reference 7: Hall JA, Roter DL, Katz NR, "Task Versus Socioemotional Behaviors in Physicians", Med Care 1987;25:399, DOI 10.1097/00005650-198705000-00004), so Reference 8 is a distinct omitted original publication.

decisions.location: Section 3.2 (Extracting articles reporting replications in TIS from BITRA, p. 14), Section 5.2 (Results of the bibliometric study, pp. 25-26), and References (p. 34)
decisions.reason: Section 3.2 explicitly describes the bibliometric study of BITRA as "carrying out a conceptual replication of Makel, Plucker, and Hegarty’s (2012) study on replication in psychology research," and Section 5.2 directly compares the replication rate, self-replication rate, and replication taxonomy proportions against Makel, Plucker, and Hegarty (2012). This target is completely distinct from shipped row 123 (Yeung, 2017, 10.3389/fnhum.2017.00468, which is replicated in Section 3.3 / 5.3) and has no DOI in the source text.
